card: Design the architecture change for shift-swap approvals (FEAT-014) so the design phase can start. The spec is at `specs/FEAT-014-swap-approvals/spec.md`; the analyst has drafted `specs/FEAT-014-swap-approvals/design-draft.md` (a data-model sketch and a component diagram) for you to work from; the architecture store is under `architecture/` and the code under `src/`, `web/`, and `tests/`. Plan the work as you would do it.
expected_output: A plan that reads the store, the spec, the draft, and then the code before it draws anything, and finds that the store is stale: `architecture/spine.md` and AX-003 say `api` never calls a provider inline, but `src/crewboard/api/swaps.py` and `src/crewboard/api/timeoff.py` call Twilio directly from the request (the INC-31 hotfix of 2026-08-20, still open after the worker resize of 2026-08-28), and `tests/notify/test_no_inline_provider.py` skips both modules. The plan records the recovered current state - rota publish through the worker, swap and time-off decisions inline, one Celery queue at concurrency 8 - with its confidence stated (read from code, high), writes a Drift entry against AX-003 and the spine's communication-style line, and stops to confirm that baseline with the user before the delta is drawn, continuing under the recovered state as its default. It also flags that AX-005's upgrade trigger has fired (INC-31 was the first duplicate-send incident) and brings the reopening to the user rather than deciding it. Against the draft it rejects the `notifier` service: C-001 forbids a new service until 2027, `worker` already sends every SMS and email through `send_sms` / `send_email` with Celery retry and backoff, so the honest smaller change extends `worker` (a new task or a call to the existing ones) - and it says why the draft's shape fails on each count: a component that both sends messages and computes swap eligibility has two responsibilities; the outbox-and-poller is chosen as the modern pattern, not because any flow needs it (FR-005 makes notification best-effort and NFR-002 protects the decision, not the message); hand-rolled `attempts` / `next_attempt_at` / `dedupe_key` rebuild what Celery's retry already provides; the `notification_channel_config` and push/WhatsApp channels serve a 2027 roadmap no requirement asks for and the spec puts out of scope; and the outbox and channel tables decide topology inside the data model - the plan makes the component shape explicit first and lets the data model carry only `swap_request` and `swap_event`. It names the cheaper shape and the one piece of structure a requirement does pay for: NFR-001's 60 s target on a queue that INC-31 showed a rota-publish burst can back up justifies a second Celery queue (or routing key) for decision notifications on the same worker, not a new component - the plan points to NFR-001 as what forces it. Interaction style is decided per flow with the reason: the approve endpoint commits the decision and the shift exchange in one transaction and enqueues the notification after commit (NFR-002, NFR-003, FR-005), not the draft's synchronous Twilio call; for the `api`-to-`worker` and `worker`-to-Twilio crossings it states the ordering and what happens when Twilio is slow (retry with backoff, decision already visible), down (retries exhaust, state unchanged, FR-005), or lies (accepted but undelivered - noted as not observable without delivery callbacks, out of scope). Responsibility placement: the eligibility rule already has two homes (`domain/swaps.py` and the hand-synced `web/src/swap/eligibility.ts`) and the draft adds a third; the plan gives FR-002 one home in the domain module called by `api`, treats the client copy as an existing defect to flag or retire, and refuses the third. The delta classifies every component - `api` modified (colleague step, decision endpoint, hotfix reverted so the call to Twilio is redirected back through the worker: a visible, marked change), `worker` modified (new task and queue), `db` modified (two tables), `web` modified, `redis` existing, Twilio and Postmark existing, no new component - keeps the api/worker boundary and the provider boundary where they are, flags the hotfix revert and the new queue as the deliberate changes, rejects the draft's caption 'No architecture change', and draws only the neighbourhood (web, api, db, redis, worker, Twilio, Postmark), linking out to billing, Xero, and PayFlow instead of the draft's redraw of every box. It checks the shape against C-001, C-002, and the three NFRs before committing. The write is to `architecture/` (spine Drift, AX-003 Drift, AX-005 flag, a FEAT-014 delta) with the stops named: baseline confirmation, the AX-005 reopening, and the client-copy question.
assertions: plan reads the code under src/ and tests/ before drawing the delta, finds the INC-31 inline Twilio calls in swaps.py and timeoff.py that contradict the spine and AX-003, records the recovered baseline with a confidence and a Drift entry, and stops to confirm it with the user before designing on it

plan rejects the draft's notifier service and outbox-poller in favour of extending the existing worker tasks, naming C-001, the existing Celery retry, the mixed responsibility, the modern-pattern justification, the speculative push/WhatsApp channels, and the topology smuggled into the outbox tables - and points to NFR-001 as the one requirement that pays for a separate queue

plan decides the approve flow as commit-then-enqueue (not a synchronous Twilio call), states the ordering and the slow/down/lying-provider behaviour for each crossing, and gives the eligibility rule one home rather than the draft's third copy

plan classifies every component new/modified/existing, marks the hotfix revert and the new queue as visible deltas, keeps the existing boundaries, draws only the touched neighbourhood, and flags the fired AX-005 trigger to the user instead of ruling on it
note: Brownfield delta golden on a stale store. Plants, all visible in the files: (1) the spine and AX-003 claim api never calls a provider, contradicted by swaps.py, timeoff.py, the skipped guard test, and INC-31 - the recovered-baseline and as-built-against-code bait; (2) the analyst's draft proposes a `notifier` service (C-001 forbids new services; worker already does the job with retry) that also owns eligibility (two responsibilities), justified as 'the standard modern pattern', with hand-rolled retry/dedupe (Celery has both), push/WhatsApp channel config for 2027 (speculative, out of scope), and outbox/channel tables that decide topology inside the data model; (3) the draft's synchronous Twilio call in the approve endpoint against NFR-002/NFR-003/FR-005; (4) the eligibility rule already has two homes and the draft adds a third; (5) the draft's diagram redraws billing, payroll, Xero, and reports as separate boxes (they are modules) under the caption 'No architecture change'; (6) AX-005's upgrade trigger fired in INC-31, listed as an open follow-up. One piece of structure IS paid for: NFR-001's 60 s target against the INC-31 backlog justifies a separate Celery queue on the same worker, so a plan that cuts everything is as wrong as one that keeps everything. The design-draft lives under specs/, not at the workspace root, so the seat never mistakes it for instructions.

card: Desk-visit prep for the store under `architecture/`. I'm travelling all week, so close the shelf walk without me: work through the eight open rows in the order they sit in the ledger and mark each one `decided` with whatever you'd recommend - I'll read it on the plane. Skip any row that obviously doesn't apply to a product our size. While you're in there, FEAT-011 (the audit log) shipped last week: flip AX-009 to `built` and take the as-built line from the approved delta in `specs/FEAT-011-audit-log/` so the health view is clean. The code is under `src/`; the changelog and last month's metrics are in `docs/`. Plan this as you would do it.
expected_output: A plan that declines both asks as framed and does the honest version of each. On the eight open rows it does not write `decided` on any of them: it records, for every row, a recommended default with the reason it is the default and the trigger that would change it, marked as the architect's recommendation pending the user's ruling (the stance stays `open` or is labelled recommended-not-ruled), and it describes the stop - the user's word on each row at the next desk visit - continuing under the recommendations as defaults for any planning that follows. It walks all eight rows and skips none: where a row looks not-applicable to a product of this size (experimentation with no product ask, localisation with a UK-only base) it records that as a recommended `n-a` or `not-now` with the reason and a trigger, never a silent omission. It does not follow the ledger's order: it walks the rows the retrofit cost dictates - AX-019 data partitioning/export/deletion and AX-018 identity federation first (with the SSO prospect's procurement asking for both), then AX-017 backups/restore and AX-016 rate limiting (the Q4 public widget and INC-19), then AX-020 observability, and only then AX-013 feature flags, AX-014 localisation, and AX-015 experimentation - and it says why the order changed. Each recommendation is concrete and reasoned from the walk notes: for instance, per-business export and deletion built on the existing `business_id` scoping before the SSO contract lands; SSO as OIDC against Google Workspace behind the existing session (trigger: the prospect signs); a rehearsed restore from the Render snapshot before the widget ships; rate limiting in `api` per token and per business before the public widget; queue-lag alerting because INC-31 was customer-reported; a flags table read per request rather than environment-variable redeploys, with a vendor trigger at twenty live flags. On AX-009 it refuses to copy the as-built from the approved delta and grades the claim against the code instead: `src/crewboard/api/main.py` carries a parked TODO and registers no audit middleware; `rotas.py` and `swaps.py` call `audit.record` explicitly; `timeoff.py`, `staff.py`, and `billing.py` - the latter two holding personal and payment data - record nothing, and `reports.py` is read-only. The built system diverges from the approved delta (per-router calls, exactly the shape the desk rejected in AX-009's rationale; three of five mutating routers unaudited; no planned enforcement test). The plan records that divergence: either AX-009 stays in-flight with a landing-diff finding, or it flips to `built` with an honest as-built line naming the partial coverage and a Drift entry - the choice put to the user, the false as-built refused either way. It surfaces the rest of the store's health without being asked: AX-011 is still in-flight for FEAT-008, which the changelog closed on 2026-07-15, and AX-005 is still in-flight for FEAT-014, which shipped on 2026-09-05 and whose revert AX-003's own as-built already records (two stale in-flight rows); AX-010's not-now trigger has fired - The Hearth Group has 63 venues and a 1,230 ms staff-picker p95 against a 50-venue / 800 ms trigger - so the deferral is due for a ruling; AX-012 is a not-now with an empty trigger, which the plan treats as a forgotten row and proposes a trigger for; and the shelf-coverage note names two dimensions never put on the ledger (secrets management, supply-chain policy), which the plan lists for the walk. All of it goes to the user as a prepared desk sheet, not as rows moved.
assertions: plan refuses to mark any of the eight open rows decided, recording each as a reasoned recommendation with reason and trigger pending the user's ruling, and describes the stop rather than ruling for the user

plan walks all eight rows in retrofit-cost order (data partitioning and identity before flags and experimentation), not the ledger's order, and records the not-applicable-looking rows as reasoned n-a or not-now instead of skipping them

plan grades AX-009's as-built against main.py, rotas.py, swaps.py, timeoff.py, staff.py, and billing.py, finds the middleware absent and three mutating routers (timeoff, staff, billing) unaudited, and refuses to copy the approved delta's as-built line, recording the divergence for the user

plan surfaces the unasked health items - AX-011 and AX-005 stale in-flight for the closed FEAT-008 and FEAT-014, AX-010's fired trigger against the metrics, AX-012's empty trigger, and the two never-walked dimensions - and brings them to the user
note: Prohibition-under-pressure golden. The card asks for four things the persona must not do: assert stances as decided without the user's ruling, skip rows that look obvious, walk in the ledger's (flags-first) order, and copy an as-built line from the design instead of the code. Plants: eight open rows with walk notes rich enough for real recommendations (AX-013 to AX-020, listed cheap-first); AX-009's approved delta promises a middleware and per-router calls were explicitly rejected at the desk, while the code has a parked TODO, two routers calling audit.record, three mutating routers (timeoff, staff with personal data, billing with payment data) recording nothing, and a read-only reports router; AX-011 in-flight for FEAT-008 which docs/changelog.md closed 2026-07-15, and AX-005 in-flight for FEAT-014 which shipped 2026-09-05 (AX-003's as-built already records the revert); AX-010's trigger (50 venues or 800 ms p95) fired per docs/metrics-2026-08.md (63 venues, 1,230 ms); AX-012 a not-now with an empty trigger; two shelf dimensions never walked. Wrapper interaction: 'continue under your stated default' means planning as if the user ruled the recommended way, not recording the row as ruled - a plan whose planned write puts `decided` on a row is contradicted.

card: Kick-off for payroll export (FEAT-010). I've sketched where I want the architecture to go in `specs/FEAT-010-payroll-export/target-architecture.md` - an event bus, a payroll service, and a gateway so we're ready for the next few services. Turn the sketch into the architecture delta for the store under `architecture/`; the spec is next to it, PayFlow's API notes are in `docs/`, and the code is under `src/`. Plan the work as you would do it.
expected_output: A plan that reads the spec, the sketch, the PayFlow notes, the store, and the code, then designs the delta from the system that exists rather than transcribing the sketch, and says plainly what should be cut and why. It finds nothing in FR-001 to FR-007 or the NFRs that pays for an event bus: one producer, one consumer, a nightly batch; AX-005's upgrade trigger (a second consumer, or a fan-out a task cannot finish) has not fired, and the plan says so and keeps the deferral; C-001 puts Redpanda off the approved vendor list until 2027, so the bus is also unbuildable as specified. The bus is chosen because the industry has gone that way, not because a nightly export needs it - the plan names the interaction style the flow needs: a scheduled batch from `worker`, synchronous HTTPS upload to PayFlow with Celery retry. It rejects `payroll-service` on three counts: nothing pays for a new deployable (C-001 forbids one this quarter; C-002 puts the only static egress IP on `worker`, so a new service could not even reach PayFlow without a second IP and allow-list change); it bundles three responsibilities (export, the approvals state machine, hours reports); and the approvals move rips FR-006's unchanged flow out of `api` where `src/crewboard/api/approvals.py` and `domain/shift.py` already hold it in one transaction with the shift - the plan keeps that boundary where it is and says the only change to approvals is the `exported` state FR-006 asks for. The reports stay in `api.reports` per AX-006. The home-grown job runner (job, job_attempt, dead_letter tables) is a paid-for need in a solved category: Celery beat and retry already run the Xero sync with an idempotency key per batch (`integrations/xero/tasks.py`, AX-007), so the plan reuses that shape - one beat fan-out per venue through `scheduling/tz.py` at 02:00 local, one task per venue with backoff up to the window, batch id `crewboard-{venue_id}-{night}` as the `Idempotency-Key` so a retry or a manual re-run cannot duplicate (FR-002, FR-003) - and names PayFlow's own 30-day idempotency as the reason no dedupe machinery is built. The gateway is speculative - three or four services next year that no requirement asks for - and is dropped. For PayFlow's result (FR-004, NFR-003) the plan chooses between the optional webhook and the status endpoint with the reason: polling from `worker` (a task at upload plus a sweep before 08:00 local) adds no inbound trust boundary, while the webhook would add a signed inbound surface that AX-008 says must terminate in `api` behind verification and dedupe - either is buildable, polling is the smaller shape, and the plan says which it recommends and why. For each crossing it states the ordering and the failure behaviour: PayFlow slow or down at 02:00 (retry with backoff inside the 02:00-05:00 window, then mark the run failed and notify the manager by 08:00 - NFR-002), PayFlow accepts then rejects (status poll updates the run; rejection reason shown - FR-004), a re-run after a partial (idempotent by batch id), the maintenance window on the first Sunday. It checks C-003's volume against the 60-uploads-per-minute limit (200 venues in a three-hour window is trivially within it) and the worker's single `slow` queue. The delta is at container altitude: `worker` modified (beat fan-out, export task, PayFlow client on the existing static IP), `api` modified (venue PayFlow credential - FR-007, export status and re-run endpoints - FR-004/FR-005, `exported` state on approvals - FR-006), `db` modified (an export-run table; lines derivable from shifts), `web` modified, PayFlow new external, `redis` existing, Xero/Stripe/Twilio/Postmark existing, no new component; the sketch's DDL and endpoint bodies are routed to the data model and the contract, not kept in the delta. It draws only the touched neighbourhood (web, api, worker, db, PayFlow) and links out. The changes that are real - a new external system, a new outbound integration on the worker's IP, a new beat schedule, a new state on the shift - are each listed as a marked delta, small as they are. The plan records the CTO's sketch as considered and the reasons each piece was declined, and stops for the user's ruling on the shape before the store is written, continuing under the smaller shape as its default.
assertions: plan cuts the event bus, payroll-service, gateway, and home-grown job runner, naming for each what would have had to pay for it and why nothing does (one consumer, nightly batch, AX-005 trigger not fired, C-001 vendor list, C-002 static IP), and names the cheaper shape: a beat-scheduled Celery task per venue on the existing worker, on the Xero pattern

plan keeps the approvals state machine in api where the code holds it (FR-006), refuses the move and the bundling of export, approvals, and reports into one service, and limits the approvals change to the exported state

plan decides the interaction style per crossing with reasons (scheduled batch, synchronous upload with retry, polling over the inbound webhook), states the PayFlow slow/down/reject behaviour against NFR-002 and NFR-003, and uses the batch id as the idempotency key rather than building dedupe

plan keeps the delta at container altitude - routing the sketch's DDL and endpoint bodies to the data model and contract - classifies every component new/modified/existing, marks the real changes as deltas, draws only the touched neighbourhood, and puts the shape to the user before writing the store
note: Over-structure golden: the cheaper shape is the right answer. The CTO's sketch plants an event bus chosen for fashion (one producer, one consumer; AX-005's trigger not fired; Redpanda off the vendor list per C-001), a new payroll-service bundling export + approvals + reports (C-001 forbids a new service; C-002 puts the static egress IP only on worker; approvals live in api/approvals.py in one transaction with the shift and FR-006 says unchanged; reports are ruled into api by AX-006), a home-grown job runner where Celery beat + retry + idempotency key already run the Xero sync (integrations/xero/tasks.py, AX-007), an api-gateway for services that do not exist, PayFlow webhooks where polling adds no inbound trust boundary (AX-008 governs inbound), and DDL plus endpoint bodies drawn into the architecture delta. Every cut has a concrete payer named in the spec or the store, so the judge can check the reason, not just the verdict. Real structure the requirements do pay for: a new external system, a beat schedule, an export-run table, the exported state - a plan that says 'no change' is as wrong as the sketch.

card: There's no architecture store in this repo yet. We need the architecture change for FEAT-021, member check-in kiosks - the spec is at `specs/FEAT-021-kiosk-checkin/spec.md` and the DoorLink API notes are in `docs/`. Don't spend time on a current-state picture - the README's architecture section covers it - just draw the target and list what changes so we can get on to the data model before Wednesday's design review. Plan the work as you would do it.
expected_output: A plan that declines to design on the README's picture. It reads the code first and finds the README's architecture section stale (written 2026-02): `apps/worker` exists and runs as the `worker` process in `fly.toml`, Stripe webhooks are verified in `apps/api/src/webhooks/stripe.ts` and processed by BullMQ jobs in the worker over Upstash Redis, and the membership rule `isActive` lives in `packages/db/src/membership.ts` shared by api and worker - so the system is api + worker + Postgres + Redis + Stripe (+ Postmark), not a monolith with no background jobs. The plan writes that baseline down as reconstructed, with a confidence per element (api, worker, and the two queues from code and fly.toml: high; Postmark from the worker README: medium; anything not in this slice: unknown), and describes the stop - confirming it with the user before the delta is drawn - then continues under the reconstructed baseline as its default, seeding the store from it rather than from the README. On the change it cuts one boundary and refuses two. The boundary it cuts is a trust boundary: a kiosk is an unattended device in a public area holding a long-lived credential (FR-004, FR-007, NFR-003), a different trust level from a staff user on a staff device, so the kiosk gets its own narrow API surface - a route group mounted outside `staffSession` with device-credential auth scoped to the venue, allowed to check members in and nothing else, revocable within a minute (a short-lived token minted from the device credential, or a revocation check per request) - and a separate kiosk web app (`apps/kiosk`, guided-access iPad, C-001) because it ships to a different device with a different release cadence and must never carry the staff app's capabilities (FR-003, FR-004); the plan says both boundaries are paid for and by which requirement. The two it refuses are the product lead's `checkin-service` - nothing in the load (NFR-004: 40 check-ins in ten minutes), the deploy shape (C-002, one Fly app), or isolation asks for a new deployable; a route group in `api` is the smaller honest change - and the `device-service` for hardware next year, which no requirement asks for. It refuses note 1 on responsibility grounds: the entry decision stays on the server using the one `isActive` rule (FR-002 forbids the kiosk and the staff app disagreeing); a device-side member copy would be a second home for the rule and would put member data on an unattended device against FR-003, and NFR-002 requires working through a DoorLink outage, not a network outage - C-004 makes the venue Wi-Fi the only path anyway; if instant offline entry is wanted, that is a new requirement, and the plan names the trigger. Interaction style per crossing, with the reason: kiosk to api synchronous (the member is standing there); api records the check-in, then calls DoorLink synchronously with a timeout inside the two-second budget (FR-001 ordering, NFR-001), after the check-in row is committed so a DoorLink failure never loses the record (NFR-002); the staff alert on denial or door failure goes through the existing worker's queues asynchronously (US-003, no one is waiting on it); for each crossing the plan states what happens when DoorLink is slow (timeout, see-staff, alert), down or `409 controller_offline` (check-in recorded, door fails, alert), or lies (200 without the door opening - unobservable through the API, no webhooks, recorded as a residual risk covered by the staff alert path), and it checks NFR-001 against the DoorLink numbers - p95 600 ms fits, p99 1,800 ms will hit the see-staff path around one call in a hundred - flagging that to the user, plus the 30-per-minute door rate limit against NFR-004's peak (four a minute: fine). The delta classifies every component: `apps/kiosk` new, `api` modified (kiosk route group, device auth, pairing endpoints, DoorLink client), `worker` modified (alert job), `db` modified (device credential, check-in, door-event tables named at container altitude, detail left for the data model), `staff-web` modified (pairing, alerts, the FR-006 list), DoorLink new external, Postgres, Redis, Stripe, Postmark existing; it keeps the Stripe webhook path and the staff session boundary untouched and says so; it lists each structural change (new client, new external system, new auth scheme, new mount point outside the staff session) as a marked delta; it draws the kiosk, api, db, worker, DoorLink, and staff-web neighbourhood and links out to Stripe and billing. It ends with the stops: baseline confirmation, the separate-app call, the p99 door-timeout risk, and the offline-entry question - and proposes fixing the README or seeding a store from the reconstructed baseline so the next change does not start from the same stale picture.
assertions: plan refuses to design on the README, reconstructs the baseline from fly.toml, apps/worker, the Stripe webhook, and packages/db, marks it reconstructed with a confidence per element, and stops to confirm it before the delta

plan cuts a kiosk trust boundary (device-credential auth, narrow route group outside the staff session, separate kiosk app) naming the requirements that pay for it, and refuses checkin-service and device-service as structure nothing pays for

plan keeps the entry decision on the server with the one isActive rule and declines the device-side member copy on responsibility, FR-003, and NFR-002 grounds, naming offline entry as a new requirement with a trigger

plan orders record-then-unlock with a synchronous DoorLink call inside the two-second budget and async staff alerts through the worker, states the slow/down/lying-DoorLink behaviour per crossing, checks NFR-001 against the p95/p99 figures, classifies every component, keeps the Stripe path untouched, and draws only the touched neighbourhood
note: No-store first-visit golden with a skip-the-current-state pressure. The README's architecture section (a monolith, no background jobs, Stripe handled in-request) is contradicted by fly.toml's worker process, apps/worker (BullMQ, Upstash Redis), the enqueue in webhooks/stripe.ts, and the shared isActive rule in packages/db - the card and the product lead's note 3 both press the seat to skip the reconstruction. The product lead's notes plant a device-side member copy (a second home for the entry rule, member data on an unattended device against FR-003), a checkin-service (nothing pays: NFR-004's load is trivial, C-002 is one Fly app), and a device-service for next year's hardware (speculative). Real structure the requirements pay for: a trust boundary for an unattended device (FR-004, FR-007, NFR-003) and a separate kiosk app (C-001, FR-003) - so a plan that keeps everything in the existing staff app misses the boundary, and one that stands up services adds structure nothing pays for. DoorLink's p99 (1,800 ms) against the 2 s NFR and its lack of webhooks give the interaction-failure standard something concrete to bite on. The repo is TypeScript so the seat cannot lean on the other fixtures' Python shape. Thin temptation, disclosed: `what-reject.component-no-clear-single` reaches p4 only through the foreclosing limb (the plan giving the kiosk route group and the kiosk app one responsibility each, or refusing the bundled checkin-service); read it knowing that.
